title: A Micro-Primer on How Motivation Works in People, Why Demoralization is So Prevalent Right Now Amongst Teachers, and What We Can Do About It
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Writing amid a pandemic-driven collapse in teacher morale, Dave Stuart Jr. lays out five principles explaining why simply telling demoralized teachers to 'get over it' never works: motivation and demotivation are products of five key beliefs (credibility, value, belonging, effort, efficacy) held in the heart rather than the intellect, which makes them powerful but hard to shift through argument alone. He illustrates the intellect-versus-belief distinction with a personal story about teaching growth mindset that raised students' questionnaire scores without changing their actual effort, arguing that beliefs are built through lived intellectual, emotional, social, and physical experience rather than being talked into existence. He reframes 2020's widespread teacher demoralization as five parallel 'crises of belief' — in credibility, value, belonging, effort, and efficacy — and argues that a crisis is a turning point that will either deepen the profession's resilience or fracture it. The piece closes by recommending a concrete application: recording a short #EducatorEncouragement video, which Stuart connects to research on attributional retraining interventions that reliably help remedy belonging-related unbelief.
points: Motivation is governed by five key beliefs — credibility, value, belonging, effort, and efficacy — held in the heart rather than the intellect, which is why merely telling someone to 'snap out of it' rarely works.

Stuart's growth-mindset teaching anecdote shows that intellectual assent to an idea (scoring well on a mindset questionnaire) can be entirely disconnected from the underlying belief needed to change behavior.
Beliefs are built through repeated intellectual, emotional, social, and physical experience — like trusting a chair after years of it holding your weight — not through a single persuasive argument.
Framing 2020's teacher demoralization as five parallel 'crises of belief' reframes an amorphous mood as an intelligible, addressable problem rather than a vague malaise.
Recording a short #EducatorEncouragement video functions as an evidence-based attributional retraining intervention that helps remedy belonging-related unbelief in both the maker and the viewer.
quotes: The start of this school year has seen a plummet in teacher morale like none I've observed before. The workload is up, the pressure is on, and the end remains hidden in the future's fog.
It is because beliefs are a kind of knowledge held not in the head but in the heart — not in the intellect, but in the will — that they are so incredibly powerful and so remarkably elusive.

Why? Because growth mindset isn't a set of intellectually assented to concepts. It's not an idea — it's a belief! A belief in effort. Until it's a thing that you know to be at the heart level, growth mindset doesn't work.
Beliefs can change. The good news, of course, is that unbeliefs can change, too.

A crisis is a turning point — after it, things can get worse, or things can get better. But, they can't stay the same. I really do think this is a turning point for our profession because so many of us are having these inner wrestling matches so intensely.

What you and I are making and participating in with these simple little videos is what the researchers call an attributional retraining intervention — the exact kind of intervention that again and again works at remedying unbelief around Belonging.
